title: Scribes
lead: Scribes began as the people who could write: royal secretaries and record-keepers. After the exile the scribe became the scholar and teacher of the law of Moses, like Ezra. In the Gospels the scribes are the experts in the law who debate with Jesus.

sections.b: Under David "The royal scribe was Seraiah" (2 Samuel 8:17): a secretary of state. Baruch "wrote on a scroll, from Jeremiah's mouth, all the words the LORD had spoken to him" (Jeremiah 36:4). After the exile Ezra was "a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6), who "had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law, to doing it, and to teaching" (Ezra 7:10). When he read the law to the people, the Levites "set out its meaning, and the people grasped what was read" (Nehemiah 8:8). Ben Sira draws the scribe's portrait in Sirach 38:24-39:11: a man of leisure for study who seeks out the law, the prophets and the proverbs, serves rulers and prays. In the Gospels Jesus teaches "as one who held authority, not as their scribes did" (Matthew 7:29), warns against "the scribes who like to go about in long robes" (Mark 12:38), and yet praises "every scribe who has learned to be a disciple of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 13:52).
